newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters agree to meet Labor Secretary Herman.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters agree to meet Labor Secretary Herman.

text.p: Teamsters union and United Parcel Service leaders agreed to meet separately with Labour Secretary Alexis Herman on Monday in the latest bid to end the eight-day strike at the nation's largest package carrier.
"I've asked leaders of the Teamsters union and the United Parcel Service to meet with me today at the Labour Department and they both agreed," Herman said in a statement.

"I intend to talk with each party individually to find out what it will take to move these talks forward and to urge greater flexibility and a willingness to compromise to get back to the bargaining table," she said.
Talks between the parties broke down Saturday despite the assistance of a federal mediator.
At the White House, President Clinton's spokesman Mike McCurry said the strike was a concern, but that the conditions for presidential intervention had not yet been met.
Herman had warned Sunday against any move by UPS to hire substitutes for striking members of the Teamsters Union and urged the two sides to resume talks without escalating the dispute.
"I believe hiring replacement workers does contribute to that escalation," Herman said on the CNN programme "Late Edition."

Executives of Atlanta-based UPS, which before the strike delivered about 80 percent of all packages shipped by ground nationwide, said they wanted to avoid hiring replacement workers but declined to rule out such a move.
"The last thing we want to do, the last thing I want to do, is replace UPS workers," Chief Executive Officer James Kelly, said on the CBS programme "Face the Nation."
But he left open the possibility, saying that UPS was losing "hundreds of millions of dollars a week."
UPS normally handles 12 million packages a day. Federal mediator John Calhoun Wells has described the strike as the "biggest" in the United States in the past 25 years.

Other package carriers have leaped into the gap left by the strike. The U.S. Postal Service said the strike was swelling its business to Christmas-season levels and added rare Sunday deliveries of packages in some places.
UPS' Kelly also said Sunday that he saw a role for President Clinton, who could suspend a strike for 30 days if it created a large enough economic emergency.
But White House spokesman McCurry said Monday that the conditions for intervention under the Taft-Hartley law had still not been met.

"The standard in the statute hasn't changed in the last week -- it's imperil the national health and safety -- and we monitor the strike conditions and the economic conditions to see if that standard has been met. So far it has not."

McCurry said the longer any strike goes on, the more economic impact it has, and the White House was concerned about that. "But we can't solve a labour/management conflict for the parties. Ultimately the two parties have to negotiate their own agreement."
